I trust that the majority in the province of Manitoba, when the time comes, and without any trouble, without raising any racial or religious issue, will bring a settlement that will satisfy the minority as we, in the province of Quebec have acted towards the Protestant minority, and as our friends in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince

Edward Island have acted towards the Acadian minority. But my friend from South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) also raised another old issue. He spoke of the plebiscite and asked the government if they had settled the question of prohibition. I would be very sorry for one that prohibition should exist, because I believe with the majority in my province, that things should remain as they are. But, I wish to protest against the remarks which fell from his lips. The hon. gentleman stated that we in our province, had been brought to the polls under the dictation of two or three members of the cabinet and that if we had been left free, probably we would have voted in favour of prohibition. In the province of Quebec we are against all excesses, the vote which was taken on the plebiscite was the true expression of the popular sentiment. We do not believe in prohibition by the statute-books, in the province of Quebec. But, let me say this to my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor), and if he does not take my word for it, he can have the word of his leader from the province of Quebec (Mr. Monk). In Quebec, with the exception of the large cities, the municipal councils are at liberty to grant licenses for hotels and restaurants, and in three-fourths of the municipalities this privilege is not used, and though we are against prohibition by statute, we are nevertheless in favour of temperance by moral suasion.
Hear, hear.
I did not say that I desired this country to participate in the wars of the empire outside Canada.

I understood my hon. friend to have said so, but of course I am ready to accept his word to the contrary. At all events, after the colonial conference which was held last summer, having read the manly answer given by my hon. friend the premier, to the proposals made by the colonial secretary, I think we should all agree that our representative did his duty. Sir, we are loyal to England. We give her the benefit of a preferential tariff. We have asked for reciprocal concessions. Whilst Mr. Chamberlain appeared to favour such a policy we find that in that respect he is somewhat isolated among the public men in Great Britain. If I were not afraid to weary the House I could quote Mr. Mor-ley, Mr. Bryce and Sir Michael Hicks-Beech on this point. It is admitted to-day that we cannot have, on the basis of protection any reciprocal trade with Great Britain. If we cannot have that mutual preference, we must fully concur in the language used by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. If Great Britain will not give us a preference then we will consider what action we shall take in the interests of Canada. Again I say that we must all approve the answer given by my right hon. friend the premier at the colonial conference. We are not ready to accept all the burdens which Mr. Chamberlain and some of his friends would like to impose on this country. As I said a moment ago, we are loyal. We are ready to do our duty to the empire, but we shall do it of our own volition. We shall do it ' proprio motu.' We will never sacrifice any of our political rights and we will never barter our political Mr. LEMIEUX (GaspS).
independence to suit the purposes of some ultra-Britishers. In a word we are and intend to remain good British subjects, but before all we are Canadians, and 1 may add that Canada belongs rightly not to a favoured few, but to all Canadians.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Before the hon gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) takes his seat, I wish to make a personal explanation. I know we would not wilfully misrepresent me. I understood him to say that I had opposed the Remedial Bill. I wish to inform the hon. gentleman that such is not the case. If he will read ' Hansard,' he will find that I both spoke and voted for the Remedial Bill. More than that, I stayed up night and day trying in every way to have the Bill passed. I always contended that the minority in Manitoba had constitutional rights, and that those rights should be recognized. By the settlement which has been made, they did not secure a recognition of those rights to which they are entitled under the constitution of our country.

I am pleased to accept the words of my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor). He may have spoken and may have voted in favour of the Remidial Bill. But it is a fact well known to every one, that, while the whip of the Conservative party, he canvassed against the Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That statement is not correct, and I ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw it.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) is probably to follow me to-night, so I shall not detain the House at any great length. I have been undecided whether to take part in this discussion, and notwithstanding your kind indulgence extended by request of hon. members permitting the whole broad subject to be discussed, taking in the financial as well as the trade question, I shall confine myself to a few words with reference to the amendment before the House. Had I desired to say anything with reference to the financial statement, I feel that it would be out of place. The statement speaks for itself. The concise, plain manner in which it was put by the hon. gentleman who delivered it, and the matter that was contained in it, render any enlargement on my part unnecessary. But if enlargement were necessary, it has been supplied by hon. gentlemen on this side who examined in more detail than did the Finance Minister the expenditures of the country. And I must say that there have been speeches delivered in this debate, and now to be found in ' Hansard ' which will be of the utmost value to me, as they will be to other hon. members, refreshing our memories for the discussion of public questions. I suppose we all feel, when we have to engage

in an election contest, after a period of rest and quiet, liow very soon we seem to forget the questions that engage our attention here.
I proceed to consider, for a few moments, then, the amendment. And it is an extraordinary position in which I find the debate on this occasion. We have an amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) which reads as follows :
That all the words after ' that ' in the proposed motion be left out, and the following *substituted therefor :-' This House regarding the operation of the present tariff as unsatisfactory is of opinion that this country requires a declared policy of such adequate protection to its labours, agricultural products, manufactures and industries as will at all times secure the Canadian market for Canadians ;
' And that the financial policy of the government should include a measure for the thorough and judicious readjustment of the tariff at the present session.'
Now, why do I say that it was a remarkable discussion that has taken place upon this amendment ? We are asked by the mover of this amendment to declare that the House regards the operation of the present tariff as unsatisfactory. I do not think that I can bring myself to vote for the amendment. But there are some hon. gentlemen in this House who can induce themselves to do so. Some of these hon. gentlemen have spoken, and have spoken at length ; but I have failed to hear any explanation as to how this tariff is unsatisfactory-not merely why it is unsatisfactory to the House, but why it is unsatisfactory to themselves. When the hon. member for West Toronto rises, I would like him to tell me what there is unsatisfactory in the working of this tariff. Is it unsatisfactory in that there has not been sufficient revenue raised to carry on the affairs of the country? The hon. gentleman will not say that, for there has been enough revenue raised under it during the years it has been in operation to more than pay the ordinary expenditure, and almost enough to pay, up to the end of the present year the ordinary and the capital expenditure. The tariff can not be unsatisfactory in that regard. Then, is it unsatisfactory in its effect upon foreign trade? I do not mean to give you many figures tonight, but I am trying to find out what is unsatisfactory in this tariff requiring the thorough revision and readjustment in all its parts called for by the amendment. Why, if the tariff requires this thorough and judicious readjustment throughout its hundreds of articles, is it not a strange thing that we have not had the defects pointed out by these hon. gentlemen. I have sat in my place patiently. The other night when the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) was lecturing the ministers for not being in their places, I did not feel guilty. I have sat here patiently and listened to what was 69
said. And now, when hon. members are asked to declare by their votes that this tariff is unsatisfactory and that it requires readjustment in all its hundreds and hundreds of articles, I say 1 shall expect the hon. member for West Toronto, who follows me, and whom I consider one of the ablest members on that side of the House, to state what has been lacking hitherto, to tell us the items in this tariff which are defective, and how they can be improved. I think we are entitled to ask that. I have asked the question whether it was unsatisfactory with reference to securing revenue and have concluded that no hon. gentleman will affirm this. Now I ask, has it been unsatisfactory as regards the promotion of foreign trade ? I have already said that I shall not give many figures, but I have here a short table in which I have divided into four six year periods the export of the produce of this country, and another in which I have divided into four six year periods the aggregate foreign trade of the country. Why did I take four six year periods ? Because, commencing with 1878 and running down through the eighteen years when the national policy came into operation, and into the six years when this tariff has been in operation. I propose to contrast the foreign trade and the progress made in building it up in three periods under the operation of the old tariff and the increase under the six years of the present tariff.
Now, the percentage of increase in the export produce of Canada for the four six-year periods between 1878 and 1892 is as follows : From 1878 to 1884 the increase was 17 per cent ; from 1884 to 1890 the increase was 7 per cent; from 1890 to 1896 the increase was 29 per cent; from 1896 to 1902 the increase was 78 per cent. Is the tariff unsatisfactory, I ask hon. gentlemen, through you, Mr. Speaker, who will follow me ? Is this tariff unsatisfactory in so far as its operations have had an effect on the exports of this country ? Well, what about the total foreign trade of this Dominion ? There are gentlemen in this House who would confine Canadian trade to Canada. They do not take views broad enough. We want Canada for the Canadians, but we want all the other countries in the world besides to sell our goods to. I do not understand that trade is a bad thing if we know how to trade. My hon. and genial friend, one of the merchant princes of this country, doing one of the largest businesses in this country, representing the city of Toronto (Mr. Brock), he does not conduct his own business on the principle that an extension of trade outside his own family would be a bad thing for him. He sends his travellers north, south, east and west. Possibly, if he confined his trade within his own family circle it might enrich the members thereof a little, but he would not do much business.
speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. ffm. Paterson).

speechtext: That is an absurdity.

Well, I see the hon. gentleman is coming to take our view of it, that trade is not a bad thing. What is a nation but an aggregate of individuals, and if it is good for an individual to trade with his neighbours, must it not he good for a nation to trade with its neighbours ? Will the hon. gentleman say it would be an absurdity ? Now, what trade have we done with other nations ? From 1878 to 1884 our total foreign trade increased 20 per cent; from 1884 to 1890 it increased 5 per cent; from 1890 to 1896 it increased 9 per cent; from 1896 to 1902 it increased 77 per cent. I ask my smiling friend opposite, when he rises to speak, to say if the tariff has been unsatisfactory in the way of promoting foreign trade.

What has the tariff had to do with the increase of the export trade of the country ?
The MINISTER OB' CUSTOMS. The tariff has had this to do with It, that when this tariff was Introduced, and it was known that it was in the hands of a government who held, as one of their fundamental principles, that changing circumstances might require in time a revision of the tariff, and that they held as a fundamental principle that the greater stability you could give to a tariff the better, from that moment the country commenced to move forward. Then I want to tell him further that by reducing the burdens of the people, immigration was promoted into this country. I want to tell him that there are more people in his country. I want to tell him that the administration of government, combined with the operations of the tariff, have had much to do with the exports. The fact that you have a cold storage system has had much to do with it; for, say what you may, you had not a cold storage accommodation to compare with the Australian, under the Conservative regime. You have it to-day, it is well known, and the figures prove, that since this government came into power the article of cheese has taken its proper place in the English market, though I do not say that it had not a good place before under hon. gentlemen opposite. But I do say that butter and other perishable products have swollen the aggregate export of the produce of this country, so far as its money value is concerned.
What did we do with our products before you came into power ? What did we do with our grain ?
A great deal of it was consumed by the people of Canada, and the balance was exported.
We had poor crops.

Well, I don't know about that. I have spoken of the eighteen years under the regime of the Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
hon. gentleman's party. Are we to understand that if the Tories came in again we are to look for another eighteen long years of bad crops ?
Whooping it up.
The hon. gentleman is getting a little irritated-

Not at all.
The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS-but I have not given him any reason; I simply point out a fact. He explains the difference by saying they had poor crops. Well, now, I say there were eighteen years when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, and that the Giver of all good blesses Canada, whether under Tory or Liberal rule, we must not forget that. And during the eighteen years they were in power, Providence smiled upon this land, as Providence has smiled upon this land since we took control of its affairs. But if it be a fact that Providence blesses this country and has blessed it, whether under Tory rule or Liberal rule, if you find an increase so vast under the Liberals that you did not find under the Tories, the same Providence being equally kind to us all, what is the inevitable inference ? Simply that while Providence blessed Canada under whatever rule it may be, the Liberals know best how to use the blessings of that Providence. That we claim for the Liberal party, and that we claim alone.
Now, Sir, I have given the facts. I have stated that there has been an entire lack of instances given us wherein this tariff is unsatisfactory. I again prefer the request that we be told how it has been unsatisfactory. It has struck me as strange in this debate that hitherto when we have had arguments upon the tariff, the old question of protection and free trade has been debated, which is not a question in actual existence in this country at all. We have been told that in certain lines the manufacturers were suffering. We had them venturing to say that certain lines were suffering, but this year, strange to say, with the resolution that these gentlemen, I presume, are about to vote for that declares that we should have a thorough and immediate revision of the tariff, we have heard very few complaints about the manufactures. What manufacturing concerns are suffering ? What manufactures do you propose to lay a duty in favour of and how much do you propose to lay. I have noticed that, leaving the manufactures alone, hon. gentlemen opposite have centered their interest upon the farming community and that it is the poor farmer they want to protect. These are the parties to whom their sympathies are extended at the present time. We have had the whip of the party, the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor), we have had the leader from the province of Ontario, the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), we have had the hon. member for

Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) and others appealing largely to the farmer and their whole argument seems to be this:	The Americans
send in here a few million dollars worth of farm products, crushing the farmers out of their market and therefore they say put up the tariff and shut the Americans out. If hon. gentlemen will bear with me for a moment I will read over the list of articles that our farmers are particularly interested in and I will show you that while the Americans do sell a few million dollars worth of their farm products, the American nation takes as large a quantity from our farmers and there is nothing to find fault with in that respect. I will just give the chief products that the farmers of this country are interested in. There are swine, horned cattle, horses, sheep, all other animals n.e.s., barley, beans, Indian corn for distillation, oats, pease, rye, wheat, bran, mill feed, &c., corn meal, oat meal, wheat flour, all other breadstuffs n.e.S, butter, cheese, hay, potatoes, turnips, vegetables canned, vegetables all other n.e.s. and eggs. Now, I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that I have gone over pretty much at any rate the important articles in which our farmers are interested and what is the result of that ? While the Americans sent into our market $2,973,098 worth in the aggregate of these articles we sent to the United States, not to other countries, but to the United States, $3,917,878 worth. They bought a million dollars worth more from our farmers of farm products than this country took of the produce of their farms, or to be exact, $944,780. But hon. gentlemen opposite will say : You have left out Indian corn, and so I may as well anticipate that there may not be any side issue in reference to it. We will take in Indian corn which we hold is on the free list for the benefit of the farmer. We think that when the manufacturer gets his raw material free, when used in the goods which he exports, the farmer and the cattle man has the right to have free corn to finish their productions. But, if we take the ground that these gentlemen take that it is an interference with our farmers and if we look at the figures we find that there were $2,480,397 worth of Indian corn imported but there was exported of that $1,036,090 worth, leaving $1,444,307 worth, and if we take the $944,780 into account we have a balance of only $499,527 in favour of the Americans. Now, I say there is not much ground for our friends to appeal to the farmers with any degree of success in that. But, they have looked into the thing very particularly and they have discovered that there are some products of the farmer that ought to be protected. The hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) dwelt upon that. He gave us, the other night, a list of fruits that came in here and he was determined to have these fruits excluded. These Yankee fruits coming in here, monopolizing our market and lowering the prices
of our own fruits was something that was not to be tolerated. He said that there was $765,771 in duty levied on these fruits that came from the United States. I had a little curiosity to look into that list and what do you think I found ? Why, that on all kinds of fruit that are grown here at present there was only a duty paid of $157,204, instead of $765,771. What did he include in the list of fruits upon which he wanted a prohibitory tariff placed ?-dried currants, dates, figs, prunes, raisins, almonds shelled, almonds, not shelled, pecans not shelled, shelled peanuts, walnuts not shelled, all other kinds of nuts, oranges, lemons and limes. Now, we must have a tariff placed upon these and it must be adequate. There is no use saying that oranges and lemons cannot be grown in this country. They can. I saw one in the hot house myself. It can be done and adequate protection, which means prohibition, if placed on oranges will tempt some people to grow a tree or two for the glory of the thing under glass. It is an outrage upon these farmers that they should be subjected to these Yankee importations of dried currants, dates, figs, prunes, raisins, almonds shelled, almonds not shelled, Brazil nuts not shelled, pecans not shelled, shelled peanuts, walnuts not shelled, all other kinds of nuts, oranges, lemons and limes. The farmers want to get even with these people and they are asking this government to put $15 more duty on the reaper that is made by the Yankee so as to get even with him in that way. That is the proposition of hon. gentlemen opposite. These Yankees send in pecans and limes and they send in some agricultural implements and it will benefit the farmer to have an additional duty of $15 placed upon his binder. Then, the hon. gentlemen took up the item of vegetables and he said that there was a duty of $86,074 laid on vegetables. He was right. That includes potatoes, tomatoes, and several other articles. I find that if it be a grudge we have against the Yankees that they took from us $327,046 worth of our potatoes while we only took from them $87,212 worth. If there is anybody who has a right to get mad about that it is the Yankees. The total value of the imports mentioned under that head were $417,407, while the people of this country exported to the United States altogether $994,410 worth, so that we sent $2 out for every one we brought in and yet this hon. gentleman is for having us engaged in a commercial war with the United States in reference to the matter, and he is going to see that these vegetables and fruits are produced in this country. Well now, if he asks my opinion, I will give him my answer. I see the smiling face of my late colleague the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) opposite me and he was good enough to say in the remarks he addressed to the House, that while he perhaps did not view me in every respect more friendly

than he did some others of his late colleagues that, at any rate, there was one question on which we were nearer perhaps than on some others.
Of course I cannot allude to these things, and I am not going to talk about ancient history. There was a speech of mine read here the other night by the member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) which I made away back in 187G, twenty-seven years ago. If the bon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) is ever here that long it will be an honour to him if lie can have a speech of his quoted which is twenty-seven years old. I was pretty young in parliament in 1876, but it is significant that the sentiments expressed at that time are those embodied in this present tariff. I said then that I did not see how a duty on wheat would help the farmer much so long as he grew a surplus and exported it, but nevertheless I said that there might be perhaps a month in the year, if the farmers were sold short and before the new crop came in, when a home demand might be required and if the farmer could import wheat under circumstances like that, then he would get the benefit And we have a duty on wheat now, and there is a duty on other grain. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) will see, therefore, that even as far back as 1876 I had sound views on the tariff, and that ought to give him confidence in any tariff that I approve of. X do not know that I would pin much faith on arguments that were used years and years ago and under different circumstances, but it just happened that in this case I announced some views about the tariff, and those views are embodied in the tariff which is in existence to-day.
Just a year ago when the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Leonard) made his motion to the effect that it was in the interest of the country that there should be an increased duty placed upon certain vegetables, the hon. the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) replied to that motion, and I commend that reply to the member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) and other gentlemen on that side of the House. The hon. gentleman from Laval moved as follows :
That it is greatly in the interest of the market gardeners and the farmers, that the duties on our Canadian garden products he so adjusted as to guarantee the Canadian farmer an effective protection against foreign competition.
I will read to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) the argument that was delivered upon that motion by my late colleague (Hon Mr. Tarte) and I think that answer will be sufficient ; I think it will show him how strange his proposition is that we should go on and increase duties on these articles because some of them are imported. The Hon. Mr. Tarte said last year :
I entertain considerable doubts as to the increase of duties on those products imported from abroad being likely to result in something practical, if you take into consideration the Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
fact that our farmers cannot supply that foreign market, because they do not produce those vegetables all the year round. Many articles, amongst those just mentioned by the hon. gentleman, are imported from the United States, to which country a little later in the year many similar products of our own are exported. If we raised the duties on those products as asked for by the hon. gentleman we should incur the risk of retaliation on the part of the United States as to products coming from Canada. We carry on, for instance, a considerable trade in melons with our neighbours, and our duty on that article is 25 per cent, whereas it is on the free list in the United States. What would my hon. friend say if the American government should decide to impose on that article a similar duty to ours ? At any rate, it is of public notoriety that the greatest number of the articles, upon which we are asked to increase the duty, are not produced in the winter months. We should thereby be increasing the prices of those products to the great mass of consumers without our market gardeners being benefited thereby. My hon. friend wants us to raise the duties upon lettuce, cucumbers, tomatoes, asparagus, celery, beets, onions.
I hope my bon. friend. (Mr. Taylor) is keeping in mind these articles, because they are the very articles which he has spoken about. The hon. gentleman continues :
It is well known that in the winter months we do not grow cabbages nor cucumbers. We are also aware that it is extremely difficult to raise tomatoes in the winter season. We had to pay, last winter, 50 cents a pound for tomatoes of Canadian growth, whilst American tomatoes were being sold on the Montreal market at 20 cents a pound.
That is the condition of things which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) wants to bring about.
Read what Mr. Tarte said after that to the effect that he was no free trader.

I am glad that my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) is following me, I have that very passage from the speech underscored here and it is curious that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) should think that I was going to miss it, because it is far more conclusive than what I have read. He says :
I am no free trader
That is a pretty well known fact.
That is true.

Now here is the point the hon. gentleman thought I was going to miss reading, and when I read it he will see that I certainly would not omit it, because it is one of the richest things in the whole speech :
I am no free trader, but it is necessary to use common sense in our transactions in this world, and I declare here and now that I object to paying 50 cents a pound for Canadian tomatoes, when I can have Amerioan tomatoes for 20 cents. It is really going too far.
Read on.

I will read on :
This shows conclusively that tomatoes cannot be grown here with advantage in the winter months. So with asparagus and cucumbers. We do not produce asparagus nor celery in the winter season. There is not to be found one single gardener in the whole island of Montreal, or around Ottawa or Toronto, who can grow lettuce as good as that imported from the United States in the winter.
Don't think you are going to get the exMinister of Public Works to vote for any such amendment as is before the Chair in favour of adequate protection, when it involves as the member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) says it does, the putting on of duties that will make twenty cent tomatoes cost fifty cents.
I ask the Minister of Customs, if the government is opposed to an increase of duty on these articles
There is no increase provided for in the tariff that is brought down this session, and as to future tariff changes of course we never announce them before the budget speech.
Hear, hear.

My excolleague (Hon. Mr. Tarte) continued to say:
It is idle to appeal to prejudices. There are enough people buying tomatoes and lettuce, for let it be known that I am speaking the plain unvarnished truth. Cauliflowers are not grown in the winter months in Canada. I agree that during a certain season of the year they can be kept, perhaps during two or three months. The cauliflowers we buy in the winter are imported from the United States.
Yet they want to put on a tariff of adequate protection to force you to pay a higher price under the circumstances which my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) describes and he seems to know whereof he was speaking :
The market gardeners around Montreal receive iust as much protection as any other class of the community does, and I may further say that those gardeners are the most prosperous people in the country.
And yet it is demanded that we should have an immediate revision of the tariff in order to benefit those poor gardeners. Here is the testimony given a year ago by the ex-minister, that these gardeners were very well off, and I am sure they have not suffered this year. The argument used by the ex-minister is an argument to show that the Liberal party in framing the tariff looked upon both sides, whereas our Couservative friends, judging by their policy and their amendment, look at only one side. They say :	Put the duties so high that it will
be prohibitory. Prohibition is the principle of their protection. That is its essence; that is its final result and our friend (Hou. Mr. Tarte) is not one of that kind because
he looks at the other side of the question as we do on this side of the House. He says:
Should I be disposed, nevertheless, to add something to their happiness, would that be conducive to the happiness of other classes of the community much more numerous than the market gardeners are.
There is where he looks; there is where the Liberal party look. They.look at all classes and all occupations; they have regard to the producer and the manufacturer, but at the same time they do not lose sight of the consumers :
To my mind, the consumers of Montreal should not be forced to pay extravagant prices for these products.
The consumers would be forced either to deprive themselves of vegetables or to pay exorbitant prices for them. Should we impose additional duties, consumers would have to pay 25 or SO per cent more, nor could we hope thereby to increase the production of those articles *which cannot be grown to advantage in this country. '
Sound sense. If, in forcing an unnatural production in this country, it should be done at the cost of raising the prices of the articles above what the people ought to pay, there would be less of them consumed, and the whole benefit would be neutralized. My hou. friend saw that clearly. He says he sees eye to eye with me on many things. He goes on to say :
There are seasons when we must import vegetables from the United States, because they can there be grown more easily and much more cheaply.
Then the hon. gentleman, who'moves the resolution, interjects this sentence :
There is this great difference, that the climate of the United States is favourable to the production of vegetables, whereas the Canadian climate is not so advantageous. And that is why our farmers ought to receive more protection than is given to the farmers in the United States.
To which the reply is made by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Public Works :
My hon. friend knows very well that, even if additional duties were imposed on pease, tomatoes, cucumbers and other vegetables, that would neither improve the climate nor enable us to grow those vegetables to advantage during the winter months. The increase in the duties asked for by my hon. friend would only result in forcing the consumer to pay more for those products, without improving the condition of the Canadian producer.
He winds up by dismissing the subject In the following words :
To my mind such a proposition is preposterous.	.
Now, my hon. friend from South Leeds would do well to ponder over that answer. There is a great deal of sense and good argument in it. There is in it the grasp of a gentleman who is considering the question, sincerely desirous as we all are that all classes in this country should prosper. But

when asked to impose duties, which, if imposed, would be of doubtful benefit even to those for whose benefit they were asked, he insists that they might so enhance prices as to lessen consumption, but if not, they would be an unjust burden placed upon those who are forced to buy the goods.
Now, I pass on to notice very briefly that when lion, gentlemen opposite ask us for a thorough and entire revision of the tariff, we should have seen a spectacle of greater agreement among themselves. I do not want to be captious. I recognize that there will be differences of opinion among hon. gentlemen opposite as to a particular rate of duty that should be placed upon a particular article. Wherever men think, you will find such differences of opinion. But here is a ease in which it appears to me professions and contradictory statements are made involving more than particular duties. For instance, the hon. member for Haltou (Mr. Henderson) and the hon. member for South Heeds (Mr. Taylor) say that they want the duty wiped off raw sugar. The hon. member for Halton said that, speaking over the head of my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), who has a refinery in his town that wants the duty on raw sugar increased. My hon. friend the leader of the Ontario opposition members in this House, the hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule) who I take it is nearer the fountain-head, if I may use that expression with reference to the hon. leader of the opposition, says that we ought to increase the duty on raw sugar, instead of taking it off. Will the lion. leader of the opposition tell us what he would do with his policy of adequate protection in that case ?

I want to correct the hon. gentleman, and say that I have no knowledge of ever having made such a statement in the House. I understood that the beet-root sugar manufacturers desired to have the duty increased on sugar, but I did not specify raw sugar at all.
They came with a deputation asking it to be increased on raw sugar.
I have given the sense of it. He said he advocated taking the duty off raw' sugar and making that up by paying a bounty.
The hon. gentleman ought to be fair enough to say that the proposal was to give it to the farmers.

Whenever a bounty is given by the Ontario government, they do not give it to the farmer in his own hand, but they so arrange it that the farmer through the manufacturer would get it; and I suppose that any government would take care that the grower of the beets would have the advantage. When the hon. member for East Grey came with that deputation, they did not ask, so far as I remember, that the bounty should be given to the farmers who grew the beets. Must I ask the hon. member if they did ?
I said there were different ways in which it could be done.
What did the deputation ask ?

I do not know, because I was1 not present until the interview was pretty well over, and therefore I did not hear many of them speak. But I said that there were two or three ways of arranging the bounty. One was by providing that the farmers should get so much a ton for their beets. Another was that there should be a bounty paid on the sugar produced according to a sliding scale: for instance, one cent per pound the first year, three-quarters of a cent the second year, one-half of a cent the third, one-quarter of a cent the fourth,, letting it run out in that way. I was not aware in what particular way the deputation wanted the assistance, but I said that the government should help them in some way, because the farmers were very much interested in the matter.
You made a speech three years ago advocating a bounty to the manufacturers.

I think the hon. gentleman will bear me out in this, that while he suggested that the bounty might be given, he did not suggest that it: might be given in the way of wiping out the duty on raw sugar.	He wanted the duty
kept on raw sugar at the same time.

No. I pointed out that the American manufacturer had a higher

duty on his sugar than the Canadian manufacturer, and therefore it was unjust to the Canadian manufacturer. I did not say in what way I advocated help, but I advocated that it should be given in some way.

I am only pointing out the difficulties incident to all tariffs, when you come down to particular items. Let me give the views of the hon. gentleman. He said :-
But those engaged in that industry want an increase in the tariff on sugars coming into the country, and for the want of this, they are handicapped in carrying on their business. We are told that unless they get some consideration in the tariff-
Mark you, Sir, this. Not by way of bounty.
-tlieir industry is likely to go down instead of becoming one of the great established industries of the country.
That is very plain. The hon. gentleman wants an increased duty on raw sugar. You do not give bounties in the tariff.
Why not ?

Because you must have a separate Act of parliament in order to do it. You do not do it because you cannot. I shall not take up longer time on this point. I merely wish to show that you cannot expect unanimity with respect to the various items in the tariff. Hon. members opposite may be able to point out that some gentlemen on this side, giving their individual views, have thought that the duty on some particular item might be raised or lowered. But those are merely personal views with regard to particular items, and these men, when asked to pronounce themselves on the tariff legislation of the country, will declare in favour of carrying out our present policy. Each bon. member recognizes that he is only one in this House, that others have their views, and he judges the tariff, not from any particular item, but taken as a whole.
Let me now say a few words on the surtax on German goods, concerning which there are as many differences of opinion among hon. gentlemen opposite as there are on the amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition. Some hon. gentlemen opposite commend us for taking the power to levy the surtax and say that it is right. Others condemn us and say that it- is wrong. Others say that we should have done it a year or two ago. Well, I hold that we were right in not doing it a year or two ago. We stand now in this position, that we have made representations to the German representatives of the German government, that we have made personal representations through our Prime Minister to the representatives of the British government, and having waited years, having given the German government ample time to turn the matter over, and they having continued to
treat us as they have done, then we put on the surtax. And the civilized world recognizes that it is a just act on the part of Canada, done at the right time.
With regard to the preferential tariff, hon. gentlemen opposite say that my hon. friend the Finance Minister, after having granted a preference, now proposes to abolish it. My hon. friend has done nothing of the kind. He has not said that he would abolish the preferential tariff. He is aware, as is every member of the government, that that is a large question in which great interests are bound up, and concerning which no hasty action should be taken. But what my hon. friend pointed out was that when in England, conferring with Mr. Chamberlain, he pointed out that while we gave a preference to Great Britain, we hoped, on the other hand, that Great Britain in return would give an exemption from the corn tax then in existence, to the colonies, but that if British statesmen continued to view our preferential tariff as of no value in itself, except as a sentiment, then we should be free to guard our own interests or to take such action as might be in our interest. There is where the preferential tariff stands.
My hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Cowan) has put in my hands a resolution in which the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) moved that there should be a bounty given to free sugar. In that resolution I find the following :
And ailso to encourage the establishment of beet sugar factories, a bounty should be offered for all beet root sugar manufactured in the Dominion during the next ten years and that the machinery necessary for such plant, not made in Canada, admitted free of duty.
But he forgot about the farmers there.
That is exactly what I said when I was with the deputation, and that is still my opinion.

The hon. gentleman has given so many contradictory opinions, some of them must be right. I say that the preferential tariff is not interfered with. There is no proposition from the Finance Minister for the abolition of a preference, but my hon. colleague has put himself in the position, as did my right hon. friend the First Minister, in that note to Mr. Chamberlain, that in view of the fact that the corn tax is now abolished, and it will not be competent for the British government to make an exception in our favour, we are at liberty to take what course we may think proper. As my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has said, the English people recognize this and would have no reason to complain if we should come to the conclusion, in our own interest, to modify, alter, amend or change that preference. There are several reasons which might prompt us to do this. We have not considered propositions from other nations. So long as the preferential tariff is in ex-

istence, if any nation should demand equal preference with Great Britain, we would not consent to give it, but if Great Britain does not consider the preference of any value to her she could not complain seriously if perhaps we desired to place ourselves in the position of being able to obtain trade preference from other nations.
My bon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) spoke in rather a scoffing way of the little we had accomplished when we went over to the mother country and asked for the preference. He seems to think that the position taken by this government on this question had something to do with our failure in that respect. At any rate he spoke in this strong language with reference to it:
But they gained nothing. But, while they gained nothing in the way of better markets, they humiliated Canada by declaring that Canada would not consider the question of imperial defence. And Canada stands as the laughing stock of the world, because, notwithstanding our wealth and position and loyalty and everything else, our premier, who was in the band wagon of the great jubilee of our lato beloved Queen in 1S97, refused to even discuss, on the lines desired, the question of imperial defence. They said Canada was not prepared to pay her share for the defence of the empire. I say this is a humiliation to Canada. We are doing less than we ought to do and are the laughing stock of the world.
There he commits himself. He says that our Canadian representatives humiliated themselves by not acceding to the views of the^ imperial government on the question of imperial defence. If he feels that this country was humiliated because the Prime Minister and his colleagues took that stand it is upon him now-and I call his attention pointedly to this-to bring up a motion in tliis House censuring tbe ministers for not having committed themselves to a policy of imperial defence upon the lines suggested by the imperial government. Now, I emphasize that, and cal] tbe attention of tbe country to it. Tbe bon. gentleman as leader of the Ontario section cannot afford to say that tbe country is humiliated, and leave it there. We want to know where the members of Ontario are upon this question ; we want to know if they feel in that position, and we can only ascertain it by a vote. The hon. gentleman may smile, but he may be in a very awkward position if he does not propose such a motion.
Now, I turn to speak of another matter and I am very glad that tbe leader of tbe opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax") has done me tbe honour of being present while I am speaking, because I wish to ask him, in all sincerity, some questions. For it has been intimated that our Conservative friends are about to bring on an election this fall. If there is an election, it is possible I may speak in one or two places, and I would like to know where we are on this question. I know where I am and where the government are, and hon. gentlemen opposite know, and so does everybody else, for tbe tariff Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
and all its items is printed, so there is no mistaking where the government stands on that point. But we have not the views of hon. gentlemen opposite; we have only this resolution which speaks of ' adequate protection.' Now, if it is not wearying the House and if the hon. leader of the opposition will not consider me unduly inquisitive-for it is in the interest of the country and of fair discussion on the platform that we should understand one another-I would ask, and ask in no carping spirit, but in all sincerity, what this means ? He will not be offended, for he has asked as direct questions across the floor. The hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) read from the report in the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' of a meeting in Morden, where the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) was asked what 'adequate protection' would signify in reference to agricultural implements. I have no doubt that what appears in ' Hansard ' is a correct copy of what appeared in the ' Telegram,' which, I believe is the organ of the Conservative party in Winnipeg. This is what is given :
Question : What about free agricultural implements promised by Mr. Macdonald ?

I will answer my friend's question before I sit down so definitely that there will be no question about It. I will answer on behalf of the Liberal-Conservative party which has no Sifton at one end and Tarte at the other.
Question : Will you raise the duty ?

We will make the duty adequate and if it is now high enough, ' as I believe it is,' to enable manufacturers to make implements in Canada, we will not increase it. I am informed that implements are as cheap .in Canada as in the United States. So the duty seems high enough.
There is a definite item on which the mover of this amendment has spoken and I ask him, in all sincerity, if that is the view lie expressed at that meeting-for he has told us that he has spoken the same in Manitoba as elsewhere.
Would the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) like me to answer now ?
If the hon. gentleman pleases.
Tn the first place l would like to.ask the Minister of Customs a question.
Oh, oh.
I suppose that if questions are to be asked at all, they are fair on both sides. Has any application been made to the government to raise the duty on agricultural implements ?
Yes.

Now, I will tell the hon. minister what I stated. Two questions were asked me on that occasion, and not one only. I was asked, in the first place, whether or not I proposed to abolish the

duty on agricultural implements, and I said that I did not, because I regarded the manufacture of these implements as a great Canadian industry and I believed the duty imposed upon implements of that character had not had the effect of. increasing the price in Canada, that I had been informed by gentlemen who had investigated the subject that the price of agricultural implements was no higher-at least was not materially higher-in Canada than in the United States.
I was asked another question-whether or not, if the Conservative party came into power, they would be prepared to raise the duty on agricultural implements; and I said that if it were necessary to preserve that great Canadian industry, I would be prepared to raise the duty on agricultural implements. I am not responsible for any report which appeared in any newspapers. I noticed the next day after the meeting that it was not reported as I have stated, and I spoke to the gentleman who represented the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' of the imperfect report of what had taken place at that meeting. The questions were proposed to me in writing, and I made exactly the answers I have stated to the House to-night.
The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS, so, we have that statement, and I think it is well that I gave the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) the opportunity to make it.
You know where you are now.
If lion, gentlemen opposite are taking the position that a statement appearing in their organ Is to be treated as untruthful, that may be all right.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) will pardon me- I am not attributing any untruthfulness, but merely saying that an imperfect report of my remarks was made, and am not casting any reflection either upon the newspapers or upon the reporter. Every one knows that where one's remarks are not written down in shorthand, they are sometimes reported in such a way as not to convey the exact meaning given. But I may tell the Minister of Customs that there are probably six or eight gentlemen here to-night who heard my remarks on that occasion and who would be prepared, if he has any doubt about the accuracy of my version, to inform him that I have stated exactly what took place. Further than that, if I had adopted the argument of th^>
hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) I might safely disregard the report of this meeting, because it had not appeared in the ' Canada Gazette.'

I certainly shall not appeal to the hon. gentleman's colleagues who were with him, for I accept the statement he has made. But he will pardon me if I say that I do not quite understand where he is now. Has
he ascertained whether these implements can be made in Canada or not ? He is asking for a thorough revision and readjustment of the tariff, and must have given close consideration to this point. Is this one of the items that he wishes to have amended ?
Oh, oh.
I think that is a fair statement. Hon. members are going to vote on this and they want to known what they are voting on.

It is perfectly right that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) should ask across the floor of this House what the policy of the opposition is. That is his position, as I understand it, that it is perfectly fair to ask what the policy of the opposition is.
Yes.

Well, let me tell him his own colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), took an entirely different position years ago, because he said that a physician should not be asked to prescribe until he had been called in to attend the patient. And Mr. Chamberlain, whom my hon. friend recognizes as a pretty high authority, took exactly the same view. Now, I am not going to shelter myself behind any such consideration as that, and I have not done so to-night. The hon. gentleman seems to think that he cannot understand our position. Well, perhaps that may be more his misfortune than his fault, I am not sure about that. I thought I had made myself pretty plain. I said that I would not take off the duty on agricultural implements, and I said further that if it were necessary to preserve this great Canadian industry I would be prepared to raise it. Now, is that not plain ? Sir, if it is necessary that an opposition should announce its policy to the country, surely it is ten times more necessary that the government should announce their policy. Now, we have in the House to-night the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs. The Minister of Customs has the floor, and he has the confidence of his colleagues. Will he answer as frankly as I have done what the policy of the government is with regard to agricultural implements ? He has told us that an application has been made to the government for an increase of duty on these implements. The government have therefore had this matter under consideration. Will the Minister of Customs now, speaking for the government to-night, tell this House and the people of this country what the policy of the government with regard to that matter is ? It will not do, Mr. Speaker, to put this answer in any evasive language. Here is a government charged with the duty of giving a tariff to this country, and I invite my hon. friend the Minister of

Customs to declare to this House and to this country, as he has seen fit to introduce this question, what the policy of the government is with regard to this application respecting agricultural implements, which he says has been under the consideration of the government ?

I have not the slightest objection to tell the hon. gentleman, and I will tell him in such definite terms that I think his own supporters will admit that he has failed to answer my question. He has not told us whether it is necessary to preserve this industry or not. I want to tell him that the propositions that the Finance Minister proposes to make are on the Table, those with which he proposes to supplement the present tariff, in which agricultural implements, binders, &c., are at 20 per cent duty, and they remain at 20 per cent. Now, that is the kind of answer he ought to be able to giye me on one item out of hundreds in the tariff ; and the evident evasion, this trimming, this cutting round, are made to enable the opposition, so far as it can, to go to the country and to say one thing here and another thing there. To say ' if it is necessary to preserve the industry '-that is not the language of gentlemen who sit behind him. It is not necessary to have more duty on to preserve the industry in the country, because there are firms making these articles.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? The constituency which I have the honour to represent, being vitally interested in the woollen industry, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he considers that the protection now afforded the woollen industry is sufficient or adequate protection ?

It is evident that the conclusion at which the ministry have arrived is that it is sufficient, as there is no change in that respect, except the German surtax. Now then, let me go on, if I am making this speech. An hon. gentleman who offers a resolution declaring that there is a necessity for an immediate and thorough revision of the tariff, when one particular item of that tariff is brought to his notice, and he is asked to give a statement, his answer was that it was dependent upon circumstances. He seems to have had that question ringing in his ears ; he must Jntve seen that that was a question in which 'the people _were interested, and he should have his mind made up on it and ascertain whether that industry could be maintained in this country or whether it could not. If he has made up his mind it cannot be maintained in this country under the present tariff, then he would say that 20 per cent on agricultural implements is not adequate protection. But I point out to him that the member for Peel (Mr. Blain) the other night read a list of iron goods that were imported . Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
from the United States amounting to some millions in value, and when he finished reading it I ventured to ask him : Why do you not read the importations of agricultural implements ? He was too wise to do that. He had heard, I fancy, something about the conversation that took place in Morden, therefore he left that out. But the member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor), honest soul that he is, blundered right into it; he read all these, and showed where there had been an increase of nearly $2,000,000 in the importation of these articles, and he said that their policy was to make the tariff so high- and hi response to one gentleman he said he didn't care if it was 100 per cent-he would make the tariff so high that every one of these articles would be made in this country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Ought to be.

He did not say that, because when I called his attention to what his leader said he replied : I don't care what my leader said, I am not responsible for that. The hon. gentleman is going to have a duty put on so that every one of these $2,000,000 worth of agricultural implements should be made in this country. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and the hon. member for Peel tells us- and I think these are gentlemen who accompanied the leader of the opposition in his trip west-have laid it down that adequate protection means that such a duty shall be put upon whatever articles that are produced and made in this country as will shut out every single article of that line coming in from another country. I want to tell the leader of the opposition that if he reads the utterances concerning the meaning of adequate protection as defined by the speeches of his lieutenants, it is beyond cavil that adequate protection means a prohibitory tariff, and nothing else. It will not be a question on the platforms of this country, if we are going to the country this fall-it will not be a question as between protection and no duties. The Liberal party never proposed to do away with all duties. The platform that was read by the hon. member tonight distinctly states that we were to raise our revenues by a tariff of customs duties. Have a tariff, but have a tariff adjusted in such a way as to weigh less heavily upon the people, and do not adjust it in such a way as to do any injury to any class. We framed our tariff upon these lines, we carried it out, and what is the use of hon. gentlemen talking about having violated our promises and our pledges ? We went to the country, and what was the result-50 of a majority.
Hear, hear.
What about Ontario ?

I want to tell hon. gentlemen that to-night we are iusisting that we shall have the information. Unless the hon. leader of the opposition gets

up now, as this is the time when this question is to be settled, and says that those were not his views that were given utterance to by his lieutenants behind defining what * adequate ' means, then, Sir, they are committed to it and what do these bon. gentlemen say ? The hon. member for South Leeds was ashed a question and he said :
Sufficient protection to secure to the manufacturers, to the agriculturists, and to the labourers of this country the work of manufacturing or producing all the articles that we can produce and manufacture in this country by our own labour and keep the money in our own country.

Hear, hear.
The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (reading)- Make your tariff sufficiently high to do that. Some hon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

Now. by inference and by what they have said I have a kind of idea what the duty will be on agricultural implements when they come iu. They are all to be made in this country. Nearly $2,000,000 worth were imported last year; that $2,000,000 worth of agricultural implements Is to be made iu this country and this is to be brought about in this way. There is $20 of a duty on a binder coming into this country now. Prior to 1895 there was a duty of $35 instead of $20, or $15 more.
Some lion.! MEMBERS. No, no.

There was $15 more duty on binders at one time and therefore we have positive proof of what is required to keep these implements or some of them out of the country, and mark you, every one is to be kept out. Binders came in and ploughs came in under a 35 per cent duty. Put the duty at 50 per cent and perhaps it will do but I question if 50 per cent will do it. They stand pledged to that. That is where they are.
Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) allow me to ask him a question ?
Yes.
Does the hon. gentleman claim that by raising tlje duty on an article he would raise the price of that article by the amount of the duty ?
Certainly.
I want an answer from the hon. Minister of Customs.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says he knows my mind as well as his own. In all cases he might not do so, but he knows as well as I do what the object of raising the duty is-and he is leading away from the question we are discussing as to what adequate protection means.
This is on the question.
Do not take me off this. In tlie case of agricultural implements 35 per cent would not shut them out of the country.
Answer.
Answer what V
The question.
I answered the question.
Oh, oh.
I answered the question.

1 would like to get a straight answer. My hon. friend has understood me. I have put to him that question to which he has given an answer already many times in my presence. Does he claim now that by raising the duty on agricultural implements we will raise the price of agricultural implements ?
I am not making that argument at all.
If my hon. friend does not contend that I have not one word to say.
I am not arguing that now, but I will say this to him that in many cases circumstances come in. These circumstances arise in individual cases and they modify-
Oh, oh.

If hon. gentleman want to laugh they may think that they can discuss this question a great deal better than I can. I have been in business myself since I was a boy. I have been actively engaged in business all my life either as an employee or an employer.
I have been in this House for thirty-one years and for twenty-seven years I have heard this question discussed, and I claim to know as much as some hon. gentlemen upon the subject. But, from the position I occupy through the kindness of the right lion, the Prime Minister in the Customs Department where I am brought into contact with the active working of the tariff and where I am brought into contact with business men I would be utterly unfit for the position, and I venture to say it myself without any egotism on my part, if I did not understand the workings of the tariff as well as any other hon. member of this House.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr.. Tarte) has asked me a.question. I want to tell him this :	When
you impose a tax you have to be very care-

ful that the incidents of that taxation is not going to be put upon the people. I atn free to tell you that, and I do not hesitate a moment to say it, that there are people m foreign countries who, in their desire to sell their goods, will sell them in this country, as they will in any other country, at a lower price than they will sell to the people in their own country. That will happen to us here and happening in this way if you have a tariff the money goes into the revenue, but, that will only go so far, but if you levy too high a tax then the consumer must pay.

Well, my hon. friend did stand a good long time. I don't want anything personal, but I may say that my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarta) was able to stand it a long time. I am standing it a little longer apparently.
Hear, hear.
I am standing by the principles on which we were elected.
No.
Yes.
We know all that.
Well then, why do you ask me ?

I have just asked a question that the hon. Minister of Customs has answered over and over again. He said a minute ago that by raising the dutv on agricultural implements we would raise the price of agricultural implements. He is wrong.

I did not say that. I ought to tell the hon. geu-tleman that he never heard me speaking that 1 know of anywhere in any different manner to that in which I am now speaking.
Hon. Mr, TARTE. The hon. minister will not deny that joublicly-I do not speak of cabinet secrets-he has advocated the raising of duties on many things and the hon. gentleman cannot stand in his place to-night and say that he is not anxious to have a higher tariff.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman says that he is not speaking about something "that transpired in the Privy Council.
No, no.

Certainly not. If we were, of course, I would be utterly precluded from saying either yes or no, because, inferentially, I would be divulging the secrets of the cabinet and I would be unworthy of occupying a position in the cabinet if I violated my oath. I think I would not so far forget myself as to violate my oath, because, if I did, credence would not be put in any statement I made. Now be ,saJ'sT that I did it openly and publicly, and if I said it openly and publicly every one knows what I said, and I stand bv what I said.
Hear, hear.
I stan where the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarti stood in reference to that fruit matter W stood in a great many other things togethei
We don't stand together now. I stand, but my hon friend (Hon. Mr. Paterson) does not stand where we stood formerly.
I do not want to have any words with my hon. friend, but if he desires any personal encounter he will find me perfectly willing to meet him either on the platform or on the floor of this House.
Hear, hear.

I grant that my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has some views on the tariff. Yes, and when he was under my tuition he got on pretty well, but when I was taken by the Prime Minister to England, he must have got playing with some bad boys in my absence- Georgie Taylor, for instance, and they must have been reading Willie Maclean's paper and so he got a little off the track.

I was playing with my hon. friend from Ontario (Mr. Ross) and some of my friends all around the government benches. I see a lot of them there, and I played with them. They would like to play again the same game if they were free to do so.

What is the matter ? Some persons seem to be uneasy. I do n it interrupt any one. However, Sir, I think it is desirable that we should keep close to this question and know what this ' adequate protection ' is.
Some hon. MEM BURS. Hear, hear.

If the hon. minister does not wish to be interrupted of course we will not interrupt him from this side of the House But he will be good enough to bear in mind that he began this game of asking questions.
The MINISTER OF CUS'l'OMS. I am not finding fault. I am pointing out to my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) that while he is a little indefinite in his own speech, and while his resolution is indefinite, he does not come out as clearly as his lieutenants have done on this matter. He heard what some of them said ; he perhaps did not hear what they all said, but unless he repudiates what was said by his lieutenants, then he must accept the responsibility of having his term 1 adequate ' interpreted by the speeches of his followers. I want to know what * adequate protection ' is, and what it means. I have pointed out that the chief Conserve-

tive whip (Mr. Taylor) has taken the ground that every agricultural implement should be made in this country, and that he would put the tariff up so high as to secure that. I put it that there was a greater increase in the imports of that particular manufactured article than in anything else, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) apparently has not been able to satisfy himself whether that industry could get along or whether it could not get along. But carrying out the policy announced by his lieutenants, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) ever has to put his ' adequate protection ' policy into operation, he will have to put the duty on agricultural implements so high that every one of them will be made in this country and none come from the outside. I have told the hon. gentleman (Mr Borden) that we had 35 per cent on agricultural implements for years, and still they came in. Thirty-five per cent may not be adequate ; it will take more, probably 50 per cent, and I question if even that would do. You take any other industry you like, and if you were to produce every article in this country then you have to have a rate of duty that would give adequate protection ; adequate protection being the prohibition of the entry of these articles into Canada. Mr. Taylor says:
My hon. friend was willing to go as high as 35 per cent.
He said that to a Liberal member who intervened in the debate.
Now I am willing to go to an amount sufficient to protect the industries of the country even if it is 100 per cent.
Then speaking of the imported agricultural implements he said :
Thus, we sent to the United States last year nearly two million dollars to purchase these implements. In a very few years there will be nothing left of them but a heap of iron, and the Americans will have our two million dollars, whereas if we had a government that would have given adequate protection, every one of these articles would have been made in this country, employment would have been given to our workingmen, Canadian farmers would be supplying the home market, and we would have these two million dollars in Canada as a national capital to help on our progress and development.
Then, according to the chief Conservative whip, under this term ' adequate protection ' there is to be a duty on agricultural implements sufficient to exclude every single one of them from being imported into this country. I pointed out that the former 35 per cent duty did not accomplish that, and he says he is willing, if it be 100 per cent, to go it. I say, Sir, that the leader of the opposition sitting there, who has assumed the responsibility of asking this House to pronounce upon this amendment, must accept that interpretation of the words ' adequate protection ' or else he must denounce it and disclaim it now. He cannot escape from it. We must know where we are in this thing.
We have an open policy ; our policy is printed ; it is in the hands of the people ; it is to be changed somewhat by the resolutions laid upon the Table, but the people know all about it. They have the right to know, if we go to the country this fall, that that will be the policy followed by us. The people know what our policy is, and they are entitled to know what the policy of the Conservatives is. Now then, there, are some other gentlemen amongst the Conservatives who have put an interpretation on this amendment. If I mistake not the member for Peel (Mr. Blain) accompanied the leader of the opposition in his journey-iugs west The member for Teel says :
A considerable quantity of these commodities come in under the present tariff, from the United States, and I submit that adequate protection should be applied to these articles that in accordance with the principles enunciated in the amendment moved by the hon. leader of the opposition, the tariff should be placed sufficiently high so that the United States farmers could not send to this country one dollar's worth of goods in competition with the products of our own farmers.
Hear, hear. I believe that.

Yes, but the hon. gentleman said more than that. He said :
That is In accordance with the principles enunciated in the amendment that Mr. Bcrdea has moved.
Hear, hear. I stand by that.

There now, we have It. The leader of the opposition has seen his lieutenant rise in this House and say : I have declared that the principle enunciated in the amendment of the leader of the oppostion when he declares for adequate protection, is a duty so high that not one single dollar's worth shall come into the country. The leader of the opposition must either acknowledge that or requdiate it. If he does not repudiate it it stands there as an explanation that the policy of the Conservative party is a prohibitory tariff.
Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) asking me a question.
No, I am making a statement. When I am through the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) can rise and say whether or not he repudiates the statements of his lieutenants.
I want the hon. gentleman to understand that I am ready to answer any question he puts.

Very well. The hon. gentleman does not require any question to be asked. I have read what the hon. member for Peel has said In regard to certain articles coming from the United States, of which he holds that not a single dollar's worth should be allowed to come into the country, and he says that is in accordance with the principle of the amend-

ment which the hon. leader of the opposition has moved. Therefore we are forced, in view of the vagueness of the language of the hon. leader of the opposition, to learn the meaning of this adequate protection from the speeches made by his supporters in the House.
Then, the hon. member for Halton is one of the old members of the House, one of the staunch old Conservatives. He told us in his speech last night:
But we say we will put a Chinese wall right round this country, and we will not allow these Americans to come in here and monopolize the markets of this country.
That is what he understands by adequate protection-a Chinese wall around this country that will admit none of those products.
Thus we have arrived at the real meaning of adequate protection ; we have learned what the policy of the Conservative party under the leadership of the hon. gentleman is to be. If not, it must be denied. It is not the old national policy ; not at all. It is to be an adequate policy that will exclude everything from this country. It is to be a prohibitive tariff as interpreted by the speeches of hon. gentlemen who are following the hon. gentleman in the House, one of whom at least in his presence has reiterated his belief that that is the true meaning of the term.
But why go to the trouble of framing a tariff with hundreds of items in it to accomplish their purpose of prohibiting the Importation of foreign goods ? Why not at once pass a simple Act and say : It shall be illegal from this time henceforth to introduce into this country any goods of which a like kind are produced in Canada. They have not thought of revenue ; there is no expression in the resolution with reference to revenue. The only thing is protection- adequate protection-which is defined to be protection high enough to exclude everything, even if it should require a duty of 100 per cent.
Well, I am glad that we have been able to have this discussion. My remarks have been a little broken up by the friendly interruptions which we have had, but I, of course, must share the responsibility of that. The hon. leader of the opposition was courteous enough to give me an answer when I asked him a question, and I endeavoured to return a like courtesy when any questions were asked of myself. I have my views on the tariff, and perhaps, like some other members in this House, I may not get what I think the very best duty on every one of the 600 or 800 items in the tariff. I am quite sure that when the hon. gentleman forms an administration in the far distant future, he will find among his supporters, possibly among his colleagues, a difference of opinion on some items, because of different interests, and so on. But we are now getting down to a principle. Hon. gentlemen Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
are not fighting for the old national policy. What they are fighting for is away beyond that. It is for a prohibitive tariff that will shut out everything, while we on this side stand where we always have stood, for a revenue tariff, and a revenue tariff is what is now enacted. It is the kind of tariff that we were instructed to frame by the great Liberal convention in 1893. We were to raise our revenues by means of a tariff, and in arranging the tariff we were to take care to do injustice to no class. We have endeavoured to do that. It is a mere play upon words to talk about protection and free trade in this country. Where you have a tariff with'hundreds of items produced in the country, where you have a constant tariff on these items, you of necessity have protection as an incident of that tariff. It cannot be otherwise, unless you put a corresponding excise duty upon the articles manufactured in the country, which no one has ever proposed. What we have contended is, that under that tariff so aranged, we had to care for every interest. We have secured a tariff for revenue. We have obtained money from the people which I believe the people have not felt the burden of to any great extent. You do not hear murmuring in the country. We are carrying on the public business, developing this country at a rate never before known. The manufacturing and farming industries especially are prospering under the operation of that tariff, as they never prospered before. And this is the time, when the country is in that prosperous condition, that you are solemnly asked to declare that it is the bounden duty of the government to have a thorough revision and readjustment of the tariff, and to have it this session.
As the hon. Finance Minister has said, under the operation of the tariff, under changing conditions, which change very fast in our time, not shutting our eyes to what is being done in the course of legislation in other countries, tariff changes may be necessitated. When the time comes when, in the opinion of the government, those changes should be made, they will be made, I believe, in such a manner, as will promote the best interests of the people of this country ; and I think the vast majority of the members of this House, and the majority of the people of this country, will feel that when the revision of the tariff becomes necessary, either in whole or in part-I believe the manufacturers themselves will feel so-that it will be safer to leave that revision in the hands of the men who completed the last revision, than to entrust it to the hands of men whose only policy, as enunciated in their speeches, is to put the duties so high as to shut out every article the like of which is produced in this country. It would be ruin to the manufacturers as well as to all other classes in the country. Every person conversant with the intricacies of a tariff levied on such a vast multi-

tude of articles as our tariff comprises, knows the interdependence of trade, the relation of one article to another ; and in-the framing of that tariff it is necessary not only to provide for securing revenue, but to see that you are not crushing out one class of manufacturers, while unduly helping another class. It is no simple matter, and I venture to express the belief that the manufacturers of this country would feel that it would be safer to have the revision of the tariff, when the time comes for it to be made, whether in whole or in part, accomplished by the men who six years ago, with the aid of their supporters in this House, put in force the tariff that has stood from that day to this, without any material change ; and during those six years there has been such prosperity in this country as never existed in it before.
